reference_calls.source_slice: In a 1955 referendum,
about 83 per cent of voters chose to keep driving on the left,
an overwhelmingly clear rejection of change.
On 10 May 1963,
however,
legislators in parliament overruled the electorate,
approving right-hand traffic from 1967 in defiance of a populace among whom the plan was unpopular.
Norway and Finland drove on the right,
with about five million border crossings a year,
so a left-hand orientation meant isolation and inconvenient journeys.
About 90 per cent of cars were left-hand drive,
so motorists overtaking on narrow two-lane highways risked head-on collisions.
A state body ran the mammoth preparation under a logo,
a large H with an arrow.
Its propaganda included a song contest on television,
and the winning jingle,
whose lyrics urged people to keep right,
reached fifth in the chart.
Some 360,000 items of signage were changed,
and a massive fleet of over 1,000 new buses with right-hand doors was procured.
A curfew kept non-essential vehicles off the asphalt from one to six,
with essential traffic exempt.
At ten to five,
all traffic stopped and crawled across,
restarting at five,
before dawn,
with its direction flipped.
Stockholm and Malmö had a longer closure,
from Saturday morning to Sunday afternoon,
while crews reconfigured junctions.
On the following Monday,
125 accidents were reported,
against 130 to 198 on earlier Mondays,
a statistical improvement put down to the heightened care of hesitant drivers.
The nervousness apparently subsided and prudent habits faded,
for by 1969 accident and fatality rates had reverted to their baseline.
